questions.stem: Chidi placed a lump of sugar crystal in a saturated sugar solution and noticed that it grew larger over a week. Which reason best explains why the crystal is NOT a living thing?
options: It does not change in size
It is not made of carbon compounds
It cannot be seen without a microscope
It grows by adding material to its outside rather than by taking in and assimilating food
questions.explanation: Living things grow from within by assimilation of food; crystals only enlarge by accretion on their surface.

questions.stem: The ability of an organism to detect and respond to changes in its surroundings is known as
questions.explanation: Irritability (sensitivity) is the response to stimuli; adaptation is a long-term fit to the environment, not an immediate response.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly shows the order of taxonomic ranks from the largest to the smallest group?
options: Kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species
Kingdom, class, phylum, order, genus, family, species
Phylum, kingdom, class, family, order, genus, species
Kingdom, phylum, order, class, family, species, genus
questions.explanation: The standard hierarchy is kingdom, phylum (division in plants), class, order, family, genus, species.

questions.stem: An organism is unicellular, has a nucleus enclosed by a nuclear membrane, and some members of its group feed by photosynthesis while others ingest food. It belongs to the kingdom
questions.explanation: Protoctists are mostly unicellular eukaryotes with both autotrophic (e.g. Euglena) and heterotrophic (e.g. Amoeba) members; Monera lack a true nucleus.

questions.stem: Mushrooms are placed in the kingdom Fungi rather than Plantae mainly because they
options: lack chlorophyll and feed by absorbing organic matter
questions.explanation: Fungi are heterotrophs that absorb food; ferns and mosses also produce spores and live in damp places, and plants also have cell walls.

questions.stem: A vertebrate has moist skin without scales, lays eggs in water and its young breathe with gills. It belongs to the class
questions.explanation: Moist naked skin and aquatic larvae with gills (tadpoles) are features of amphibians such as toads and frogs.

questions.stem: Which of the following plants produces seeds that are NOT enclosed in an ovary?
questions.explanation: Pine is a gymnosperm with naked seeds on cone scales; the others are angiosperms whose seeds develop inside an ovary (fruit).

questions.stem: Which of the following is a feature of plants but NOT of animals?
options: Growth occurs mainly at the tips of roots and shoots throughout life
questions.explanation: Plants grow at apical meristems throughout life; animals grow all over the body and growth is usually limited. Mitochondria, respiration and food storage occur in both.

questions.stem: Hydra is often described as being at the tissue level of organisation because it
options: is made of a colony of identical cells
has cells grouped into two layers that perform different functions but has no true organs
questions.explanation: Hydra has an ectoderm and endoderm (tissues) but no true organs or organ systems.

questions.stem: The leaf of a plant is regarded as an organ because it
options: is made up of a single kind of cell
is made up of several tissues working together to perform particular functions
questions.explanation: An organ is a structure composed of different tissues (epidermis, mesophyll, vascular tissue) working together.

questions.topic: Complexity of organization in higher organisms
questions.stem: One disadvantage of increasing complexity of organisation in higher organisms is that
options: the organism can perform many functions efficiently
there is division of labour among cells
cells become so specialised that they cannot survive on their own
the organism becomes larger in size
questions.explanation: Specialised cells depend on other cells; damage to one system can affect the whole organism. Division of labour and efficiency are advantages.

questions.topic: Forms in which Living Cells Exist
questions.stem: Spirogyra is described as filamentous because its cells are
options: joined end to end in an unbranched chain
questions.explanation: Spirogyra cells are joined end to end to form long unbranched filaments.

questions.stem: Which of the following structures is present in a typical plant cell but absent from a typical animal cell?
questions.explanation: Only plant cells have a cellulose cell wall; the other structures occur in both.

questions.stem: The structure in an animal cell that contains digestive enzymes which can break down worn-out organelles is the
questions.explanation: Lysosomes are membrane sacs of hydrolytic enzymes used in intracellular digestion and autolysis.

questions.stem: A cell that produces and secretes large amounts of a protein hormone is likely to have a large amount of
options: rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus
questions.explanation: Proteins are made on rough ER and packaged for secretion by the Golgi apparatus.

questions.stem: Under a light microscope, the eyepiece lens of a microscope is marked x10 and the objective lens x40. The total magnification of the image is
questions.explanation: Total magnification = eyepiece magnification x objective magnification = 10 x 40 = 400.

questions.stem: A drawing of a cell is 60 mm long. If the actual length of the cell is 0.15 mm, the magnification of the drawing is
questions.explanation: Magnification = drawing length / actual length = 60 / 0.15 = 400.

questions.stem: Red blood cells were placed in a solution and after some time they swelled and burst. The solution was
questions.explanation: In a hypotonic solution water enters by osmosis; animal cells lack a wall, so they swell and burst (haemolysis).

questions.stem: When a plant cell is placed in a concentrated sugar solution, the cytoplasm shrinks away from the cell wall. This condition is called
questions.explanation: Water leaves by osmosis and the protoplast pulls away from the wall: plasmolysis.

questions.stem: Root hair cells absorb mineral ions from the soil even when the concentration of the ions is higher inside the cells. This is possible by
questions.explanation: Uptake against a concentration gradient requires energy from respiration: active transport.

questions.stem: Strips of raw yam of equal length were placed in sugar solutions of different concentrations for one hour. A strip that showed no change in length was in a solution that was
questions.explanation: No net water movement means the external solution has the same water potential as the cells.

questions.stem: Which of the following would INCREASE the rate of diffusion of a substance into a cell?
options: Increasing the thickness of the membrane
Reducing the surface area of the cell
questions.explanation: A steeper gradient, larger surface area, thinner membrane and higher temperature all speed diffusion.

questions.stem: Amoeba obtains its food by
options: absorbing digested food through its cell wall
filtering water through an oral groove lined with cilia
engulfing food particles with pseudopodia to form a food vacuole
questions.explanation: Amoeba is holozoic: it engulfs prey by phagocytosis and digests it in a food vacuole. The oral groove is a feature of Paramecium.

questions.stem: During vigorous exercise, an athlete develops cramps in the leg muscles. This is caused by the accumulation of
questions.explanation: When oxygen supply is insufficient, muscle respires anaerobically, producing lactic acid that causes fatigue and cramp.

questions.stem: Aerobic respiration of one molecule of glucose yields much more energy than anaerobic respiration because
options: glucose is completely oxidised to carbon dioxide and water
aerobic respiration occurs only in the cytoplasm
questions.explanation: In aerobic respiration glucose is fully broken down; in anaerobic respiration much energy remains locked in ethanol or lactic acid.

questions.stem: The oxygen debt built up during strenuous exercise is repaid by
options: continued deep breathing after exercise to oxidise the lactic acid
converting carbon dioxide to oxygen in the muscles
producing more ethanol in the muscles
questions.explanation: After exercise, extra oxygen is taken in to oxidise lactic acid (or convert it back to glucose in the liver).

questions.stem: The respiratory quotient (RQ) is the ratio of carbon dioxide produced to oxygen used. For the complete oxidation of glucose, C6H12O6 + 6O2 -> 6CO2 + 6H2O, the RQ is
questions.explanation: RQ = 6 CO2 / 6 O2 = 1.0. Fats have an RQ of about 0.7 and proteins about 0.9.

questions.stem: In Amoeba, carbon dioxide and ammonia are removed mainly by
questions.explanation: Small waste molecules diffuse out across the large surface area; the contractile vacuole mainly removes excess water.

questions.stem: The main function of the contractile vacuole in a freshwater protozoan such as Paramecium is to
options: remove excess water that enters by osmosis
questions.explanation: Freshwater is hypotonic to the cytoplasm, so water enters; the contractile vacuole expels it (osmoregulation).

questions.stem: Which of the following factors is an internal factor that affects growth?
questions.explanation: Hormones (e.g. auxins, growth hormone) are internal; light, temperature and water are external factors.

questions.stem: The process by which cells become specialised to perform particular functions is called
questions.explanation: After division, cells differentiate, changing structure to carry out specific functions.

questions.stem: The streaming of cytoplasm that forms pseudopodia in Amoeba is an example of
questions.explanation: Amoeboid movement involves cytoplasmic flow into extensions called pseudopodia.

questions.stem: The growth of a pollen tube towards the ovule in response to chemicals is an example of
questions.explanation: A tropism directed by chemicals is chemotropism.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of asexual reproduction?
questions.explanation: Binary fission involves one parent and produces genetically identical offspring; conjugation, pollination and fertilisation are sexual processes.

questions.stem: An advantage of sexual reproduction over asexual reproduction is that it
options: produces large numbers of offspring quickly
produces offspring identical to the parent
produces offspring with variation that may survive changing environments
questions.explanation: Sexual reproduction mixes genes, creating variation useful for adaptation and evolution.

questions.topic: Skeleton and supporting systems in animals
questions.stem: Which of the following bones forms part of the pectoral girdle of a mammal?
questions.explanation: The pectoral girdle consists of the scapula and clavicle; the ilium is part of the pelvic girdle.

questions.topic: Skeleton and supporting systems in animals
questions.stem: A vertebra that has a large, flat centrum, short neural spine and transverse processes fused with ribs to form a broad bone that articulates with the pelvic girdle is a
questions.explanation: Sacral vertebrae are fused to form the sacrum, which joins the pelvic girdle.

questions.topic: Skeleton and supporting systems in animals
questions.stem: The atlas vertebra differs from other vertebrae because it
options: has no centrum and supports the skull, allowing nodding
has a long neural spine for muscle attachment
questions.explanation: The atlas lacks a centrum and has large facets for the occipital condyles; the odontoid process belongs to the axis.

questions.stem: The supporting tissue in plants whose cells have walls thickened at the corners with cellulose and pectin is
questions.explanation: Collenchyma has living cells with corner thickenings; sclerenchyma has dead lignified cells.

questions.stem: Lignin, which strengthens xylem vessels and sclerenchyma fibres, makes the cells
questions.explanation: Lignified cells lose their contents and become hard, rigid and impermeable.

questions.stem: The wall of the left ventricle is thicker than that of the right ventricle because the left ventricle
options: pumps blood to all parts of the body at high pressure
pumps blood to the lungs only
questions.explanation: The left ventricle must generate greater pressure to send blood around the systemic circulation.

questions.stem: Mammalian red blood cells are well suited for carrying oxygen because they
options: are biconcave, lack a nucleus and contain haemoglobin
can pass out of capillaries into tissues
questions.explanation: A biconcave shape gives a large surface area, and absence of a nucleus leaves more room for haemoglobin.

questions.stem: Veins differ from arteries in that veins
options: have valves and thinner walls with a wider lumen
carry blood away from the heart
questions.explanation: Veins carry blood at low pressure towards the heart, so they have thin walls, wide lumen and valves to prevent backflow.

questions.stem: A person of blood group O can donate blood to people of all blood groups because the red cells of group O
options: have both A and B antigens
have no antibodies in the plasma
have no A or B antigens
questions.explanation: Group O red cells carry neither antigen A nor B, so they are not agglutinated by recipient antibodies.

questions.stem: A man has a heart rate of 75 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 70 cm^3. His cardiac output in one minute is
questions.explanation: Cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume = 75 x 70 = 5250 cm^3 per minute.

questions.topic: Uptake and movement of water and mineral salts in plants
questions.stem: In the root, water moves from the root hair to the xylem by passing through the
questions.explanation: Water crosses the cortex, then the endodermis, then the pericycle into xylem.

questions.stem: The transport of manufactured food from the leaves to other parts of the plant is called translocation and takes place in the
questions.explanation: Sugars (mainly sucrose) and amino acids move in phloem sieve tubes.

questions.stem: A ring of bark including the phloem was removed from the stem of a woody plant. After some weeks, the bark just above the ring was swollen. This shows that
options: water moves upwards in the phloem
food moving downwards in the phloem accumulated above the cut
minerals move downwards in the xylem
questions.explanation: Ringing removes phloem; downward-moving sugars collect above the ring, causing swelling, while xylem water flow continues.

questions.stem: A cobalt chloride paper turned from blue to pink faster on the lower surface of a leaf than on the upper surface. This shows that
options: the lower surface has more stomata
the upper surface has a thinner cuticle
the lower surface has more chloroplasts
the upper surface absorbs more water
questions.explanation: Dry cobalt chloride is blue and turns pink with water; faster change below indicates more stomata on the lower surface.

questions.stem: Plants of dry regions such as cacti reduce water loss by
options: having many large stomata on both surfaces
having leaves reduced to spines and a thick waxy cuticle
opening stomata during the hottest part of the day
questions.explanation: Spines reduce transpiring surface area and the thick cuticle limits evaporation.

questions.topic: Movement of water to the apex of trees and herbs
questions.stem: The main force that pulls water up to the top of tall trees is
options: transpiration pull together with cohesion of water molecules
questions.explanation: Evaporation from leaves creates tension; cohesion and adhesion maintain a continuous water column in xylem.

questions.topic: Movement of water to the apex of trees and herbs
questions.stem: Water oozing from the cut stump of a well-watered plant is evidence of
questions.explanation: Root pressure pushes water up the xylem and makes it exude from cut stems.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a feature of an efficient respiratory surface?
questions.explanation: Respiratory surfaces must be thin and moist for gases to dissolve and diffuse; a thick dry surface is unsuitable.

questions.stem: The vital capacity of a student is 3500 cm^3 and the residual volume is 1200 cm^3. The total lung capacity is
questions.explanation: Total lung capacity = vital capacity + residual volume = 3500 + 1200 = 4700 cm^3.

questions.stem: The excretory organ of the earthworm is the
questions.explanation: Earthworms excrete through paired nephridia in each segment; Malpighian tubules belong to insects and flame cells to flatworms.

questions.stem: In insects, nitrogenous waste is removed mainly as uric acid by the
questions.explanation: Malpighian tubules extract waste from the haemolymph and pass it to the hindgut; uric acid conserves water.

questions.stem: Which of the following pairs of excretory products and organs is correctly matched in a flowering plant?
options: Oxygen - leaf stomata during the day
questions.explanation: Green plants give off oxygen, a by-product of photosynthesis, through stomata; plants store many wastes in old leaves and bark.

questions.stem: In a nephron, small molecules such as glucose, urea and salts are forced out of the blood under high pressure into the
options: loop of Henle from the surrounding capillaries
collecting duct from the renal vein
questions.explanation: High pressure in the glomerulus forces small molecules into Bowman's capsule.

questions.stem: Glucose is normally absent from the urine of a healthy person because it is
options: completely reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule
too large to be filtered at the glomerulus
converted to urea in the kidney
questions.explanation: Glucose is filtered but all of it is actively reabsorbed in the proximal tubule. Glucose in urine suggests diabetes mellitus.

questions.stem: Excess amino acids in mammals are broken down in the liver by a process called
questions.explanation: Deamination removes the amino group, which forms ammonia then urea in the ornithine cycle.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a function of the mammalian liver?
options: Storage of glycogen and production of bile
Filtration of blood to form urine
questions.explanation: The liver stores glycogen, makes bile, deaminates proteins and detoxifies; insulin and amylase come from the pancreas.

questions.stem: On a hot day, the body temperature of a human is lowered when
options: sweat evaporates from the skin and arterioles in the skin dilate
the arterioles in the skin constrict
questions.explanation: Evaporation of sweat removes latent heat, and vasodilation sends more blood to the surface to lose heat.

questions.stem: A boy aged 14 suddenly ran from a barking dog. His heart beat faster and his pupils dilated. The hormone mainly responsible is
questions.explanation: Adrenaline from the adrenal medulla prepares the body for "fight or flight".

questions.stem: Insulin lowers blood glucose level by
options: increasing the absorption of glucose in the gut
stimulating the kidney to retain glucose
promoting conversion of glucose to glycogen in the liver and muscles
questions.explanation: Insulin from the beta cells of the islets of Langerhans stimulates glucose uptake and glycogen formation.

questions.stem: The bending of a shoot towards light is caused by
options: auxin accumulating on the lit side, causing more growth there
gibberellin destroying cells on the shaded side
ethylene speeding growth on the lit side
auxin accumulating on the shaded side, causing more growth there
questions.explanation: Auxin moves to the shaded side and stimulates cell elongation, so the shoot curves towards light.

questions.stem: The plant hormone that promotes the ripening of fruits such as banana and plantain is
questions.explanation: Ethylene is a gaseous hormone that triggers fruit ripening.

questions.stem: Which plant hormone promotes stomatal closure and seed dormancy?
questions.explanation: Abscisic acid is a stress hormone that closes stomata during water shortage and maintains dormancy.

questions.stem: Breathing and heartbeat are controlled by the
questions.explanation: The medulla oblongata contains the respiratory and cardiac centres.

questions.stem: The myelin sheath around an axon
options: insulates the axon and speeds up the conduction of impulses
questions.explanation: Myelin insulates and allows impulses to jump between nodes of Ranvier, increasing speed.

questions.stem: Quickly removing your hand from a hot pot is an example of
questions.explanation: It is rapid, automatic and does not need prior learning; it is coordinated by the spinal cord.

questions.stem: The correct sequence of structures in a reflex arc is
options: effector, motor neurone, relay neurone, sensory neurone, receptor
receptor, motor neurone, relay neurone, sensory neurone, effector
receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, effector
sensory neurone, receptor, relay neurone, effector, motor neurone
questions.explanation: The impulse passes from the receptor along sensory, relay and motor neurones to the effector.

questions.stem: A dog that salivates on hearing the sound of a bell that was always rung before feeding is showing
questions.explanation: The response to a previously neutral stimulus is learned through association: a conditioned reflex.

questions.stem: When a person looks from a distant object to a near one, the
options: ciliary muscles relax, the suspensory ligaments tighten and the lens becomes thinner
iris dilates the pupil to let in more light
ciliary muscles contract, the suspensory ligaments slacken and the lens becomes more convex
retina moves forward towards the lens
questions.explanation: For near vision, ciliary muscles contract, tension on the lens is reduced and it becomes fatter to bend light more.

questions.stem: Short sight (myopia) can be corrected by wearing spectacles with
questions.explanation: In myopia the image forms in front of the retina; a diverging lens moves it back onto the retina.

questions.stem: The three small bones in the middle ear transmit vibrations from the eardrum to the
questions.explanation: The ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) amplify vibrations and pass them to the oval window of the cochlea.

questions.stem: Which part of the ear is concerned with balance?
questions.explanation: The semicircular canals (with utriculus and sacculus) detect head movement and position.

questions.stem: The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the
options: pharynx, to equalise air pressure on both sides of the eardrum
questions.explanation: Opening of the Eustachian tube (e.g. when swallowing) equalises pressure across the tympanum.

questions.stem: A woman has a regular 28-day menstrual cycle and her last menstruation began on day 1. Ovulation is most likely to occur around
questions.explanation: In a 28-day cycle ovulation usually occurs about 14 days before the next period, i.e. around day 14.

questions.stem: The hormone that maintains the thickened lining of the uterus after ovulation is
questions.explanation: Progesterone from the corpus luteum maintains the endometrium for implantation.

questions.stem: The life cycle of the cockroach is described as incomplete metamorphosis because
options: there is a pupal stage between larva and adult
it has only an adult stage
there is no pupal stage; the egg hatches into a nymph that resembles the adult
questions.explanation: Incomplete metamorphosis: egg, nymph, adult. Complete metamorphosis includes larva and pupa.

questions.stem: Which of the following insects undergoes complete metamorphosis?
questions.explanation: Butterflies have egg, larva (caterpillar), pupa and adult stages; the others have nymphs.

questions.stem: Which of the following vertebrates shows internal fertilisation and lays eggs with a hard shell?
questions.explanation: Birds fertilise internally and lay shelled eggs; toads and most fish fertilise externally; rabbits are viviparous.

questions.stem: Animals that produce very large numbers of eggs, such as toads and fish, usually
options: provide little or no parental care, so many offspring die
incubate their eggs in a nest
questions.explanation: Large numbers compensate for high mortality when there is external fertilisation and little parental care.

questions.stem: A flower in which the ovary is positioned above the attachment of the other floral parts is described as having a
questions.explanation: In hypogynous flowers such as hibiscus, sepals, petals and stamens arise below the ovary.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a feature of a wind-pollinated flower?
options: Feathery stigma hanging outside the flower
questions.explanation: Wind-pollinated flowers (e.g. maize, grasses) have exposed feathery stigmas and light, smooth pollen.

questions.stem: Cross-pollination is favoured in a flower in which
options: the anthers and stigma mature at the same time
the stamens mature before the stigma is receptive
the stigma lies directly below the anthers
questions.explanation: Protandry (stamens maturing first) prevents self-pollination and favours cross-pollination.

questions.topic: Development of the zygote in flowering plants
questions.stem: In flowering plants, the fusion of a male nucleus with the two polar nuclei (or the diploid central nucleus) produces the
questions.explanation: Double fertilisation: one male nucleus fuses with the egg (zygote, 2n), the other with the polar nuclei (endosperm, 3n).

questions.topic: Development of the zygote in flowering plants
questions.stem: The integuments of the ovule develop into the
questions.explanation: Integuments become the seed coat (testa); the micropyle remains as a small pore.

questions.stem: A fruit that develops from a single flower with several free carpels, such as the custard apple, is called
questions.explanation: An aggregate (etaerio) fruit forms from free carpels of one flower; a multiple fruit, like pineapple, forms from many flowers.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a false fruit because parts other than the ovary develop with it?
questions.explanation: In cashew the swollen "apple" is the receptacle/pedicel; the true fruit is the nut.

questions.stem: A dry fruit which splits along two sides to release its seeds, as in cowpea, is a
questions.explanation: Legumes are dehiscent fruits splitting along both sutures.

questions.stem: Fruits of the balsam and of the African oil bean (Pentaclethra) are dispersed by
questions.explanation: The pods dry unevenly and split violently, flinging seeds away.

questions.stem: In photosynthesis, the oxygen released comes from
questions.explanation: Photolysis of water in the light stage releases oxygen; carbon from CO2 is used to make sugar.

questions.stem: A destarched potted plant had one leaf enclosed in a flask containing potassium hydroxide solution and was left in sunlight. The leaf later gave a negative starch test because
options: potassium hydroxide absorbed the carbon dioxide in the flask
questions.explanation: KOH absorbs CO2, so photosynthesis could not take place in that leaf.

questions.stem: When testing a leaf for starch, it is boiled in alcohol in order to
options: kill the cells and stop all reactions
remove the chlorophyll so that the colour change can be seen
questions.explanation: Boiling in water kills and softens; alcohol extracts chlorophyll so the blue-black iodine colour is visible.

questions.stem: The light-independent (dark) reactions of photosynthesis take place in the
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide fixation (Calvin cycle) occurs in the stroma using ATP and NADPH from the grana.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a limiting factor of photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Light, CO2 and temperature limit the rate; oxygen is a product, not a raw material.

questions.stem: Yellowing of leaves (chlorosis) in a maize plant could be due to deficiency of
questions.explanation: Magnesium is part of chlorophyll and nitrogen is needed for chlorophyll and proteins; lack of either causes chlorosis.

questions.stem: In water culture experiments, the purpose of the control set-up is to provide
options: a complete nutrient solution against which deficient solutions are compared
questions.explanation: The control plant receives all essential elements, so differences in test plants can be traced to the missing element.

questions.stem: A child whose diet is mainly cassava and yam with little protein is likely to suffer from
questions.explanation: Kwashiorkor results from protein deficiency even when carbohydrate intake is adequate.

questions.stem: A food sample was heated with Benedict's solution and gave a brick-red precipitate. The sample contains
questions.explanation: Benedict's test gives a green-yellow-brick red precipitate with reducing sugars such as glucose.

questions.stem: Pepsin works best in the stomach because
options: bile is present in the stomach
the temperature in the stomach is higher than elsewhere
the stomach contents are acidic due to hydrochloric acid
questions.explanation: Pepsin has an optimum pH of about 2, provided by gastric HCl.

questions.stem: Bile aids digestion of fats by
options: converting fats to fatty acids and glycerol
emulsifying fats into tiny droplets, increasing surface area for lipase
questions.explanation: Bile salts emulsify fats; bile contains no digestive enzymes.

questions.stem: An enzyme stopped working after being boiled because
options: high temperature denatured the protein, changing the shape of its active site
questions.explanation: Enzymes are proteins; heat destroys their 3D structure and active site irreversibly.

questions.stem: An organism that obtains nutrients from dead and decaying organic matter is called a
questions.explanation: Saprophytes such as mushrooms secrete enzymes onto dead matter and absorb the products.

questions.stem: Dodder (Cuscuta) attaches to host plants and absorbs food through haustoria. Its mode of nutrition is
questions.explanation: Cuscuta is a total stem parasite drawing food and water from the host's vascular tissue.

questions.stem: The main function of the human large intestine (colon) is
options: absorption of water and mineral salts
questions.explanation: Most nutrients are absorbed in the ileum; the colon reabsorbs water, forming faeces.

questions.stem: The dental formula of an adult human is i 2/2, c 1/1, pm 2/2, m 3/3. The total number of teeth is
questions.explanation: Teeth on one side: 2+1+2+3 = 8 upper and 8 lower = 16; multiplied by 2 for both sides = 32.

questions.stem: A mammal with the dental formula i 0/3, c 0/1, pm 3/3, m 3/3 is most likely a
options: herbivore such as a cow or goat
questions.explanation: Absence of upper incisors and canines (replaced by a horny pad) and a diastema are features of ruminant herbivores.

questions.stem: The carnassial teeth of a dog are specialised for
questions.explanation: Carnassials (last upper premolar and first lower molar) slide past each other like scissors to cut flesh.

questions.stem: In Paramecium, food particles are directed into the gullet by
options: beating of cilia in the oral groove
questions.explanation: Cilia lining the oral groove sweep bacteria and particles into the cytostome.

questions.stem: In an ecosystem, bacteria and fungi that break down dead organisms are important because they
options: convert oxygen into carbon dioxide only
release nutrients back into the soil for use by plants
questions.explanation: Decomposers recycle minerals such as nitrogen and phosphorus back to the soil.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an edaphic factor?
questions.explanation: Edaphic factors relate to soil (texture, pH, water content, humus).

questions.stem: Which of the following factors is most likely to limit the growth of plants on the floor of a dense tropical rainforest?
questions.explanation: The closed canopy intercepts most light, so light is limiting at ground level.

questions.stem: The instrument used to measure the turbidity (clarity) of water in a pond is the
questions.explanation: A Secchi disc is lowered until it disappears; the depth indicates water clarity.

questions.stem: In the food chain: grass -> grasshopper -> lizard -> hawk, the lizard is a
options: primary consumer at the second trophic level
producer at the first trophic level
tertiary consumer at the fourth trophic level
secondary consumer at the third trophic level
questions.explanation: Grass (T1, producer), grasshopper (T2, primary consumer), lizard (T3, secondary consumer), hawk (T4).

questions.stem: A pyramid of numbers may be inverted in a food chain such as
options: many grasses -> fewer grasshoppers -> fewer lizards
many algae -> fewer tadpoles -> one fish
many maize plants -> fewer rats -> one snake
one mango tree -> many caterpillars -> many parasitic wasps
questions.explanation: A single large producer supports many small herbivores, and parasites outnumber their hosts, so the pyramid of numbers is not upright.

questions.stem: Only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is passed on to the next. If producers in a pond fix 50 000 kJ of energy, the amount likely to reach the secondary consumers is about
questions.explanation: 50 000 x 0.1 = 5000 kJ to primary consumers; 5000 x 0.1 = 500 kJ to secondary consumers.

questions.stem: Food chains rarely have more than four or five links because
options: energy is lost at each trophic level, so too little remains to support further levels
questions.explanation: Energy lost as heat in respiration, in faeces and uneaten parts limits the length of food chains.

questions.stem: The relationship between leguminous plants and Rhizobium bacteria in their root nodules is an example of
questions.explanation: Both benefit: the bacteria fix nitrogen for the plant and receive carbohydrates and shelter.

questions.stem: Cattle egrets follow grazing cattle and feed on insects disturbed by them, while the cattle neither gain nor lose. This association is
questions.explanation: One partner benefits and the other is unaffected: commensalism.

questions.stem: Mangrove plants growing in waterlogged swamps of the Niger Delta obtain oxygen for their roots through
options: tap roots that go deep into the mud
questions.explanation: Pneumatophores grow upwards out of the mud and have lenticels for gaseous exchange.

questions.stem: Sulphur dioxide released from burning fossil fuels contributes mainly to
questions.explanation: SO2 dissolves in rain water to form acids that damage plants, buildings and lakes.

questions.stem: Gas flaring in oil fields releases large quantities of carbon dioxide which contributes to
options: global warming through the greenhouse effect
questions.explanation: CO2 traps outgoing infrared radiation, raising global temperatures.

questions.stem: When fertiliser washes from farms into a lake, rapid growth of algae occurs followed by death of fish. This sequence is called
questions.explanation: Nutrients cause algal blooms; when the algae die, bacterial decomposition uses up oxygen and fish die.

questions.stem: Biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) of a river is high when the river
options: contains much organic sewage being decomposed by microorganisms
has a high population of fish
questions.explanation: Decomposers use dissolved oxygen to break down organic matter, so polluted water has a high BOD.

questions.stem: The gradual and orderly change in the species composition of a community over time is called
questions.explanation: Succession is the replacement of one community by another until a stable climax is reached.

questions.stem: The first organisms to colonise bare rock in primary succession are usually
questions.explanation: Lichens can survive on bare rock and begin weathering it, forming a thin soil for mosses and later plants.

questions.stem: Secondary succession differs from primary succession in that it
options: begins on an area where soil is already present, such as an abandoned farm
questions.explanation: Secondary succession occurs where a community has been removed but the soil remains, so it is faster.

questions.stem: Which of the following would cause an increase in the population of a species in a habitat?
questions.explanation: Population grows when natality plus immigration exceed mortality plus emigration.

questions.stem: In a sigmoid population growth curve, the stationary phase is reached when
options: birth rate is far greater than death rate
birth rate equals death rate as limiting factors operate
there is no competition for food
questions.explanation: Environmental resistance (food, space, disease) balances births and deaths at the carrying capacity.

questions.stem: Salting fish preserves it because salt
options: draws water out of microorganisms by osmosis, preventing their growth
questions.explanation: The high solute concentration dehydrates microbes and inhibits enzyme activity.

questions.stem: The social insect in which a colony has a queen, king, workers and soldiers, and which builds mounds in the savanna, is the
questions.explanation: Termites live in colonies with castes and build mounds; bees and wasps lack a king.

questions.stem: The use of ladybird beetles to reduce the population of aphids on crops is an example of
questions.explanation: Using a natural predator to control a pest is biological control.

questions.stem: A disadvantage of using persistent chemical pesticides such as DDT is that they
options: are cheap and easy to apply
accumulate along food chains and harm non-target organisms
break down rapidly in the soil
questions.explanation: Persistent pesticides are not broken down and become concentrated at higher trophic levels (bioaccumulation).

questions.stem: Houseflies spread typhoid and cholera mainly by
options: carrying germs on their legs and mouthparts from faeces to food
questions.explanation: Houseflies are mechanical vectors that transfer pathogens from dirt and faeces to uncovered food.

questions.stem: Which microorganism is used in making bread rise?
questions.explanation: Yeast ferments sugar, producing carbon dioxide which makes the dough rise.

questions.stem: The souring of palm wine after some days is mainly due to
questions.explanation: Acetic acid bacteria oxidise ethanol to ethanoic (acetic) acid, making the wine sour.

questions.stem: Antibiotics such as penicillin are effective against diseases caused by
options: fungi growing on the skin only
questions.explanation: Antibiotics act on bacterial structures and processes; they do not cure viral infections.

questions.stem: Vaccination protects a child against measles by
options: stimulating the body to produce antibodies and memory cells against the virus
killing the virus directly in the blood
giving ready-made antibodies from a horse
increasing the number of red blood cells
questions.explanation: A vaccine induces active immunity: the immune system produces antibodies and memory cells.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a function of public health authorities?
options: Treating individual patients in private clinics only
Ensuring proper disposal of refuse and sewage
questions.explanation: Public health covers sanitation, refuse and sewage disposal, safe water, food inspection and disease surveillance.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a method of conserving wildlife?
options: Bush burning to drive out animals
Establishing game reserves and national parks
questions.explanation: Protected areas such as Yankari Game Reserve and Cross River National Park conserve habitats and species.

questions.stem: Planting trees on land that has never been a forest is called
questions.explanation: Afforestation is planting trees where there was no forest; reafforestation replants a cleared forest.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of continuous variation in humans?
questions.explanation: Height shows a range of intermediate values (normal distribution); the others fall into distinct groups.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a physiological variation in humans?
options: Blood groups of the ABO system
questions.explanation: Blood groups, tongue rolling and ability to taste PTC are physiological differences; skin colour, height and nose shape are morphological.

questions.stem: The physical appearance of an organism resulting from its genetic make-up and environment is its
questions.explanation: Genotype is the genetic make-up; phenotype is the observable characteristic.

questions.stem: In guinea pigs, black coat (B) is dominant over white (b). When two heterozygous black guinea pigs are crossed, the expected ratio of black to white offspring is
questions.explanation: Bb x Bb gives BB, 2Bb, bb: three black to one white.

questions.stem: A test cross is carried out by crossing an organism showing the dominant phenotype with
questions.explanation: If any offspring show the recessive trait, the tested parent must be heterozygous.

questions.stem: A tall pea plant crossed with a dwarf pea plant produced 48 tall and 46 dwarf offspring. The genotype of the tall parent was most likely
options: either TT or Tt; it cannot be told
questions.explanation: A 1:1 ratio results from Tt x tt; a TT parent would give all tall offspring.

questions.stem: Which of the following events occurs in meiosis but NOT in mitosis?
options: Pairing of homologous chromosomes and crossing over
questions.explanation: Synapsis and crossing over in prophase I are unique to meiosis; DNA replication and spindles occur in both.

questions.stem: A couple already have three daughters. The probability that their fourth child will be a son is
questions.explanation: Each birth is independent: the father produces X and Y sperms in equal proportion, so the chance is always 1/2.

questions.stem: Two parents are both carriers (AS) of the sickle-cell allele. The probability that their child will have the genotype SS is
questions.explanation: AS x AS gives AA, AS, AS, SS; one in four is SS.

questions.topic: Linkage, sex determination and sex-linked characters
questions.stem: In humans, the sex of a child is determined by
options: the type of chromosome in the egg
the type of sex chromosome in the sperm that fertilises the egg
the number of autosomes in the sperm
questions.explanation: All eggs carry X; a sperm carrying X gives a girl (XX) and one carrying Y gives a boy (XY).

questions.topic: Linkage, sex determination and sex-linked characters
questions.stem: A woman who is a carrier of haemophilia (XHXh) marries a normal man (XHY). The probability that a son of theirs will be haemophiliac is
questions.explanation: Sons receive Y from the father and one X from the mother: half get Xh and are haemophiliac.

questions.stem: Crossing two different pure breeds of poultry to obtain offspring that grow faster and lay more eggs than either parent makes use of
questions.explanation: Hybrids of unrelated pure lines often show heterosis, i.e. superior performance.

questions.stem: Genetic counselling before marriage is advised for intending couples who are both AS mainly to
options: reduce the chance of having children with sickle-cell anaemia
determine the sex of their children
questions.explanation: Two AS parents have a 1 in 4 chance of an SS child with each pregnancy.

questions.stem: In a honeybee colony, the members that collect nectar, build the comb and feed the larvae are the
questions.explanation: Workers are sterile females that do all colony work; drones mate with the queen.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an advantage of social life in animals such as termites and bees?
options: Each individual must perform every task
Division of labour and better protection of the colony
Less competition for mates within the colony
questions.explanation: Castes specialise in tasks such as feeding, defence and reproduction, increasing efficiency and survival.

questions.stem: The presence of similar bones in the forelimb of a bat, the flipper of a whale and the arm of a human is evidence of evolution from
questions.explanation: Homologous structures share a basic plan inherited from a common ancestor but are adapted to different uses.

questions.stem: Lamarck's theory of evolution is based on
options: natural selection and survival of the fittest
use and disuse and the inheritance of acquired characteristics
questions.explanation: Lamarck proposed that characteristics acquired by use or disuse are passed on; Darwin proposed natural selection.

questions.stem: According to Darwin's theory, the main reason why some individuals survive and reproduce more than others is that
options: they possess favourable variations that suit them to the environment
they acquired new characteristics during life
they are larger than the others
questions.explanation: Natural selection favours heritable variations that improve survival and reproduction.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a statement of the cell theory?
options: All living things are made up of cells, and new cells arise from pre-existing cells
Cells arise spontaneously from non-living matter
questions.explanation: Schleiden, Schwann and Virchow established that cells are the basic units of life and arise from existing cells.

questions.topic: Irritability as a Basic Characteristic of Protoplasm
questions.stem: The response of a whole free-moving organism such as Euglena towards light is called
questions.explanation: Taxis is movement of a whole organism in response to a directional stimulus; tropism is growth of part of a plant.

questions.topic: Irritability as a Basic Characteristic of Protoplasm
questions.stem: The folding of the leaflets of Mimosa pudica when touched is an example of
questions.explanation: Nastic movements are non-directional responses; Mimosa leaflets fold whatever the direction of the touch.

questions.stem: Which of the following conditions results from the hardening of salts such as calcium oxalate in the kidney?
questions.explanation: Crystallised salts form stones (calculi) that may block the urinary tract.

questions.stem: Excessive consumption of alcohol over a long period can damage the liver, causing
questions.explanation: Cirrhosis is scarring of liver tissue, often linked to chronic alcohol abuse or hepatitis.

questions.stem: The receptors for smell in humans are located in the
options: olfactory epithelium in the roof of the nasal cavity
questions.explanation: Olfactory cells in the upper nasal cavity detect chemicals dissolved in mucus.

questions.stem: Food appears tasteless when a person has a heavy cold mainly because
options: much of the flavour of food depends on the sense of smell, which is blocked
the taste buds are destroyed by the cold
questions.explanation: Flavour is a combination of taste and smell; mucus blocks the olfactory receptors.

questions.stem: The fingertips are more sensitive to touch than the back of the hand because the fingertips have
options: more touch receptors per unit area
questions.explanation: Sensitivity depends on the density of receptors such as Meissner's corpuscles.

questions.stem: The display of colourful tail feathers by a peacock in front of a peahen is an example of
questions.explanation: Courtship displays attract and stimulate a mate of the same species.

questions.topic: Metamorphosis and life history of housefly
questions.stem: The correct sequence of stages in the life history of the housefly is
questions.explanation: Houseflies undergo complete metamorphosis; maggots develop in decaying matter.

questions.topic: Adaptive features in a developing animal
questions.stem: The yolk in the egg of a bird is important to the developing embryo because it
options: provides food for the growing embryo
questions.explanation: Yolk is the food store; albumen cushions and supplies water and protein; the allantois stores waste.

questions.stem: In epigeal germination, as in cowpea, the cotyledons
options: are carried above the soil by the elongation of the hypocotyl
questions.explanation: In epigeal germination the hypocotyl elongates and lifts the cotyledons above ground; in hypogeal (e.g. maize) they stay below.

questions.stem: Which set of conditions is necessary for seed germination?
options: Water, oxygen and a suitable temperature
questions.explanation: Seeds need water, oxygen and warmth; many germinate without light or soil.

questions.stem: The conversion of ammonium compounds to nitrites and then to nitrates by bacteria is called
questions.explanation: Nitrosomonas oxidises ammonium to nitrite and Nitrobacter oxidises nitrite to nitrate.

questions.stem: Which bacteria return nitrogen from the soil to the atmosphere?
options: Bacteria of decay that produce ammonia
questions.explanation: Denitrifying bacteria reduce nitrates to nitrogen gas, especially in waterlogged soils.

questions.topic: Modes of Nutrition (autotrophic, chemosynthetic and carnivorous plants)
questions.stem: Carnivorous plants such as the pitcher plant trap insects mainly to obtain
options: nitrogen compounds that are scarce in their soils
questions.explanation: They grow in nitrogen-poor soils and digest insects to obtain nitrogen; they still photosynthesise.

questions.topic: Modes of Nutrition (autotrophic, chemosynthetic and carnivorous plants)
questions.stem: Nitrifying bacteria obtain energy to make food by oxidising inorganic compounds. Their mode of nutrition is
questions.explanation: Chemosynthetic autotrophs use energy from chemical reactions rather than from light.

questions.stem: In ruminants such as the cow, cellulose is digested with the help of
options: cellulase produced by the salivary glands
questions.explanation: Mammals cannot make cellulase; bacteria and protozoa in the rumen digest cellulose.

questions.stem: Which of the following animals is a filter feeder?
questions.explanation: Mosquito larvae use mouth brushes to filter small particles from water.

questions.stem: The mouthparts of a housefly are adapted for
questions.explanation: The housefly has a proboscis with a spongy labellum; it pours saliva on food and sucks up the liquid.

questions.topic: Ecological Components: Lithosphere, Hydrosphere, Atmosphere and Niche
questions.stem: Two species of birds feed in the same tree, but one eats insects on the bark while the other eats fruits. They avoid competition because they occupy different
questions.explanation: Same habitat, different roles (niches), so there is little direct competition.

questions.stem: A quadrat is most suitable for estimating the population of
questions.explanation: Quadrats sample stationary or slow-moving organisms; mobile animals are estimated by capture-recapture.

questions.stem: In a capture-recapture study, 40 snails were marked and released. Later, 50 snails were caught, of which 10 were marked. The estimated population of snails is
questions.explanation: Population = (first catch x second catch) / marked recaptured = (40 x 50) / 10 = 200.

questions.stem: Ten quadrats each of area 1 m^2 were thrown in a field and a total of 30 Tridax plants were counted. The estimated density of Tridax is
questions.explanation: Density = total number / total area sampled = 30 / 10 m^2 = 3 per m^2.

questions.stem: According to the laws of thermodynamics applied to ecosystems,
options: energy is not created or destroyed, but at each transformation some is lost as heat
energy is recycled through an ecosystem like nutrients
energy increases at each trophic level
questions.explanation: Energy flows one way through an ecosystem and is degraded to heat; nutrients, not energy, are recycled.

questions.stem: Which of the following processes REMOVES carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis fixes CO2 into organic compounds; the other processes release CO2.

questions.stem: In the water cycle, water vapour is released from plants into the atmosphere by
questions.explanation: Plants lose water vapour through stomata; condensation forms clouds and precipitation returns water as rain.

questions.topic: Ecological Management: Tolerance, Minimum and Maximum Range
questions.stem: The range of an environmental factor between the minimum and maximum within which an organism can survive is called its
questions.explanation: Outside the tolerance range the organism cannot survive; growth is best around the optimum.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an adaptation of the water lily to its aquatic habitat?
options: Thick waxy cuticle on the lower surface of the leaf
Deep tap root to reach underground water
Large air spaces in the stem and leaves for buoyancy
questions.explanation: Aerenchyma provides buoyancy and stores air; stomata are on the upper surface of floating leaves.

questions.stem: Which of the following trees is characteristic of the Guinea savanna of Nigeria?
questions.explanation: Parkia biglobosa and shea butter trees are common in the Guinea savanna; mangroves grow in coastal swamps.

questions.stem: If all the snakes in a farm were killed, the most likely immediate effect would be
options: a decrease in the rat population
an increase in the rat population and more damage to crops
an increase in the number of hawks
questions.explanation: Removing a predator allows its prey to multiply, upsetting the balance in nature.

questions.stem: Knowledge of the life cycle of a crop pest helps the farmer mainly to
options: apply control measures at the most vulnerable stage of the pest
questions.explanation: Targeting the stage most easily killed (e.g. larvae) improves control and reduces costs.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an application of biology to improve crop yield?
options: Planting the same crop every season on the same land
questions.explanation: Plant breeding produces high-yielding, disease-resistant varieties such as improved cassava varieties.

questions.topic: Microorganisms: Man and His Health (Nigeria extension)
questions.stem: Which of the following diseases is caused by a virus?
questions.explanation: Polio is viral; tuberculosis is bacterial, malaria protozoan and ringworm fungal.

questions.topic: Microorganisms: Man and His Health (Nigeria extension)
questions.stem: Cholera is best prevented by
options: drinking safe, treated water and proper disposal of faeces
questions.explanation: Cholera bacteria spread through water and food contaminated by faeces.

questions.stem: Before blood transfusion, the blood groups of donor and recipient are matched in order to
options: prevent agglutination of red blood cells in the recipient
increase the haemoglobin of the donor
determine the sex of the recipient
questions.explanation: Mismatched transfusions cause antibodies in the recipient to agglutinate donor red cells.

questions.stem: Competition between individuals of the same species for food and space is called
questions.explanation: Intra = within one species; inter = between different species.

questions.stem: The long, sticky tongue of the chameleon is a structural adaptation for
questions.explanation: The chameleon shoots out its long sticky tongue to capture insects at a distance.

questions.stem: Bright, contrasting colours of some poisonous caterpillars that discourage predators are called
questions.explanation: Aposematic (warning) colours signal distastefulness or toxicity.

questions.stem:
(a) Name the five kingdoms of living organisms and give one named example of each. [10 marks]
(b) State three features each that distinguish members of the kingdom Fungi from members of the kingdom Plantae. [6 marks]
(c) Explain the meaning of binomial nomenclature, using one named organism as an example. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Monera, e.g. Escherichia coli / Rhizobium / Nostoc
2 marks: (a) Protoctista (Protista), e.g. Amoeba / Paramecium / Euglena
2 marks: (a) Fungi, e.g. Rhizopus / Mucor / mushroom (Agaricus) / yeast
2 marks: (a) Plantae, e.g. maize / hibiscus / fern / moss
2 marks: (a) Animalia, e.g. toad / earthworm / goat (1 mark kingdom, 1 mark example in each)
6 marks: (b) Fungi: no chlorophyll / heterotrophic (absorb food); cell wall of chitin; body of hyphae (mycelium); store glycogen; Plantae: have chlorophyll / photosynthesise; cellulose cell wall; store starch; roots, stems and leaves (any three contrasting pairs, 2 marks each)
2 marks: (c) Each organism is given two Latin names: the genus (capital initial) followed by the species (lower case), written in italics or underlined
2 marks: (c) Correct example, e.g. Homo sapiens: Homo = genus, sapiens = species
questions.explanation: (a) Monera (Rhizobium), Protoctista (Amoeba), Fungi (Rhizopus), Plantae (maize) and Animalia (toad). (b) Fungi lack chlorophyll and absorb ready-made organic food, have chitin cell walls, are built of hyphae forming a mycelium and store glycogen; plants have chlorophyll and make their own food, have cellulose walls, store starch and are differentiated into roots, stems and leaves. (c) Binomial nomenclature, introduced by Linnaeus, names each organism with a genus name and a specific name, e.g. Homo sapiens for man; the genus begins with a capital letter and both are italicised or underlined.

questions.stem:
(a) With the aid of a list, state five structures found in a plant cell and give one function of each. [10 marks]
(b) Give four differences between a plant cell and an animal cell. [4 marks]
(c) A student viewed onion epidermal cells under a microscope with an eyepiece of x10 and an objective of x10, and drew one cell 50 mm long. If the actual length of the cell is 0.25 mm: (i) calculate the magnification of the drawing; (ii) state the total magnification of the microscope. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: (a) Any five structure + function pairs, 2 marks each: cell wall - support/shape; cell membrane - controls entry and exit of substances; nucleus - controls cell activities / carries genetic material; cytoplasm - site of chemical reactions; chloroplast - photosynthesis; mitochondrion - respiration/energy release; vacuole - stores cell sap / maintains turgidity; ribosome - protein synthesis
4 marks: (b) Any four, 1 mark each: plant cell has cellulose cell wall, animal cell has none; plant has chloroplasts, animal none; plant has large central vacuole, animal small or none; plant stores starch, animal glycogen; plant regular shape, animal irregular; animal has centrioles, plant (higher) lacks them
1 mark: (c)(i) Magnification = drawing length / actual length
1 mark: (c)(i) = 50 / 0.25
2 marks: (c)(i) = x200
2 marks: (c)(ii) Total magnification = 10 x 10 = x100
questions.explanation: (a) Cell wall gives shape and support; cell membrane is selectively permeable; nucleus controls cell activities and contains chromosomes; chloroplasts trap light for photosynthesis; mitochondria release energy in respiration; the vacuole stores sap and keeps the cell turgid. (b) Plant cells have a cellulose wall, chloroplasts, a large central vacuole and store starch; animal cells lack these, store glycogen and have centrioles. (c)(i) Magnification = 50 / 0.25 = x200. (ii) Microscope magnification = 10 x 10 = x100.

questions.stem:
(a) Define (i) osmosis; (ii) active transport. [4 marks]
(b) Describe an experiment using a fresh pawpaw or yam tissue to demonstrate osmosis. [8 marks]
(c) State four differences between diffusion and active transport. [4 marks]
(d) Explain why a fresh vegetable such as ugu (fluted pumpkin) leaf becomes soft when salt is sprinkled on it. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) Osmosis: movement of water molecules from a dilute solution (high water potential) to a concentrated solution (low water potential) across a selectively permeable membrane
2 marks: (a)(ii) Active transport: movement of substances across a membrane against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration (ATP)
2 marks: (b) Peel a yam/pawpaw and cut a cup (hollow) in it; cut the base flat; remove any skin
2 marks: (b) Place concentrated sugar solution in the cup and mark the level with a pin; stand the cup in a dish of water
1 mark: (b) Set up a control using a boiled yam cup
2 marks: (b) After some hours the level of solution in the cup rises; no rise in the boiled control
1 mark: (b) Conclusion: water passed into the cup by osmosis through living cells, which act as a selectively permeable membrane
4 marks: (c) Any four, 1 mark each: diffusion needs no energy, active transport needs energy (ATP); diffusion down a gradient, active transport against it; diffusion occurs in living and non-living systems, active transport only in living cells; active transport needs carrier proteins; active transport is affected by respiratory inhibitors/oxygen supply, diffusion is not
2 marks: (d) Salt dissolves in surface water forming a concentrated (hypertonic) solution
2 marks: (d) Water leaves the leaf cells by osmosis; cells become plasmolysed/flaccid and lose turgidity, so the leaf softens
questions.explanation: (a) Osmosis is movement of water from a region of high water potential to low water potential through a selectively permeable membrane; active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient using energy. (b) A yam cup containing sugar solution is set in water with a boiled-yam control; the solution level rises only in the living cup, showing osmosis through living cell membranes. (c) Diffusion is passive, down a gradient and occurs in non-living systems; active transport uses ATP and carriers, goes against a gradient, occurs only in living cells and stops when respiration is inhibited. (d) Salt forms a hypertonic solution on the leaf, water leaves the cells by osmosis and the cells become flaccid, so the leaf wilts and softens.

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between aerobic and anaerobic respiration. [4 marks]
(b) Write a word equation for anaerobic respiration in (i) yeast; (ii) human muscle. [4 marks]
(c) Describe an experiment to show that germinating seeds produce carbon dioxide. [8 marks]
(d) State two industrial uses of anaerobic respiration by yeast in Nigeria. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) Aerobic uses oxygen, anaerobic does not; aerobic gives complete breakdown to CO2 and water, anaerobic incomplete (ethanol/lactic acid); aerobic releases much more energy; aerobic occurs partly in mitochondria, anaerobic in cytoplasm (any two contrasting points, 2 marks each)
2 marks: (b)(i) Glucose -> ethanol + carbon dioxide + (little) energy
2 marks: (b)(ii) Glucose -> lactic acid + (little) energy
2 marks: (c) Put soaked germinating seeds in flask A and boiled (dead) seeds sterilised with antiseptic in flask B as control
2 marks: (c) Connect each flask to a tube dipping into lime water (or bicarbonate indicator); close the flasks so only the seed gas passes through
1 mark: (c) Leave for some hours at room temperature
2 marks: (c) Lime water connected to germinating seeds turns milky (indicator turns yellow); control remains clear
1 mark: (c) Conclusion: germinating seeds release carbon dioxide in respiration
4 marks: (d) Any two, 2 marks each: brewing beer/burukutu/pito; production of ethanol (industrial alcohol); baking bread (CO2 raises dough); production of palm wine/gin distillation
questions.explanation: (a) Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and breaks glucose down completely to carbon dioxide and water in the mitochondria, releasing much energy; anaerobic respiration occurs without oxygen in the cytoplasm, the breakdown is incomplete and little energy is released. (b) Yeast: glucose -> ethanol + carbon dioxide + energy. Muscle: glucose -> lactic acid + energy. (c) Germinating seeds in one flask and boiled, sterilised seeds in a control flask are each connected to lime water; only the lime water from the living seeds turns milky, showing CO2 is produced. (d) Brewing of beer and local drinks, baking of bread and production of industrial alcohol.

questions.stem:
(a) Describe the double circulation of blood in a mammal, naming the chambers of the heart and the main blood vessels involved. [10 marks]
(b) State three structural differences between an artery and a vein. [6 marks]
(c) Name two components of blood and give one function of each. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Deoxygenated blood from the body enters the right atrium through the venae cavae
2 marks: (a) It passes through the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle, which pumps it through the pulmonary artery to the lungs (pulmonary circulation)
2 marks: (a) Oxygenated blood returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium and passes through the bicuspid valve into the left ventricle
2 marks: (a) The left ventricle pumps blood through the aorta to all parts of the body (systemic circulation)
2 marks: (a) Blood passes through the heart twice in one complete circuit; semilunar valves prevent backflow into ventricles
6 marks: (b) Any three, 2 marks each: artery has thick muscular/elastic wall, vein thin wall; artery narrow lumen, vein wide lumen; artery has no valves (except at base), vein has valves; artery blood under high pressure and pulsates, vein low pressure
4 marks: (c) Any two, 2 marks each: red blood cells - carry oxygen (haemoglobin); white blood cells - defend against disease (phagocytosis/antibodies); platelets - blood clotting; plasma - transports dissolved food, hormones, CO2, urea and heat
questions.explanation: (a) Deoxygenated blood from the venae cavae enters the right atrium, passes the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle and is pumped through the pulmonary artery to the lungs. Oxygenated blood returns in the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, passes the bicuspid valve into the left ventricle and is pumped into the aorta to the body. Blood passes through the heart twice per circuit, hence double circulation. (b) Arteries have thick, elastic, muscular walls, a narrow lumen, no valves and high, pulsating pressure; veins have thin walls, a wide lumen, valves and low pressure. (c) Red cells carry oxygen; white cells fight infection; platelets help clotting; plasma carries dissolved substances.

questions.stem:
(a) What is transpiration? [2 marks]
(b) Explain how each of the following affects the rate of transpiration: (i) humidity; (ii) wind; (iii) temperature; (iv) light intensity. [8 marks]
(c) Describe how a potometer can be used to compare the rate of water uptake by a leafy shoot in still air and in moving air. [6 marks]
(d) State two importance of transpiration to plants. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Loss of water in the form of vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through the stomata
2 marks: (b)(i) High humidity reduces the water vapour gradient between leaf and air, so rate decreases (low humidity increases it)
2 marks: (b)(ii) Wind removes saturated air around the leaf, maintaining a steep gradient, so rate increases
2 marks: (b)(iii) High temperature increases evaporation and lowers air humidity, so rate increases
2 marks: (b)(iv) Light opens stomata, so rate increases in bright light
2 marks: (c) Cut a leafy shoot under water and fit it airtight into the potometer filled with water; introduce an air bubble into the capillary tube
2 marks: (c) Measure the distance moved by the bubble in a fixed time in still air; reset the bubble with the reservoir
2 marks: (c) Repeat with a fan blowing on the shoot; the bubble moves faster in moving air, showing faster uptake/transpiration
4 marks: (d) Any two, 2 marks each: creates transpiration pull for movement of water and mineral salts; cools the plant; helps distribution of water to cells; removes excess water
questions.explanation: (a) Transpiration is loss of water vapour from aerial parts, mostly through stomata. (b) High humidity lowers the rate by reducing the diffusion gradient; wind raises it by removing humid air; high temperature raises it by speeding evaporation; light raises it by opening stomata. (c) A shoot cut under water is fitted into a potometer; the distance an air bubble moves per minute is recorded in still air and then with a fan; faster movement with the fan shows wind increases water uptake. (d) Transpiration provides the pull that lifts water and minerals, cools the leaves and distributes water.

questions.stem:
(a) Describe the structure of a nephron. [6 marks]
(b) Explain how urine is formed in the mammalian kidney under the headings: (i) ultrafiltration; (ii) selective reabsorption. [8 marks]
(c) Explain the role of the kidney in osmoregulation when a person drinks very little water on a hot day. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Bowman's capsule (cup-shaped) enclosing a knot of capillaries, the glomerulus, supplied by afferent and drained by efferent arterioles
2 marks: (a) Proximal (first) convoluted tubule leading to the loop of Henle in the medulla
2 marks: (a) Distal (second) convoluted tubule opening into a collecting duct; the tubule is surrounded by capillaries
2 marks: (b)(i) Afferent arteriole is wider than the efferent, creating high pressure in the glomerulus
2 marks: (b)(i) Water, glucose, salts, urea and amino acids are forced into Bowman's capsule as glomerular filtrate; blood cells and large proteins remain
2 marks: (b)(ii) In the proximal tubule all glucose, amino acids and much water and salts are reabsorbed into the blood (actively/osmosis)
2 marks: (b)(ii) Further water is reabsorbed in the loop of Henle, distal tubule and collecting duct; the remaining fluid with urea and excess salts is urine
2 marks: (c) Water loss in sweat raises the concentration of blood (osmotic pressure); detected by the hypothalamus
2 marks: (c) Pituitary gland releases more antidiuretic hormone (ADH)
2 marks: (c) ADH makes distal tubules and collecting ducts more permeable; more water is reabsorbed; small volume of concentrated urine is produced
questions.explanation: (a) A nephron consists of Bowman's capsule around the glomerulus, a proximal convoluted tubule, the loop of Henle, a distal convoluted tubule and a collecting duct, all surrounded by capillaries. (b) Ultrafiltration: high pressure in the glomerulus forces water and small solutes into the capsule. Selective reabsorption: glucose, amino acids, most salts and water return to the blood from the tubules, leaving urea and excess water as urine. (c) On a hot day with little drinking, blood becomes concentrated; the hypothalamus stimulates the pituitary to release more ADH, which increases water reabsorption in the collecting ducts, giving a small volume of concentrated urine.

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between endocrine and exocrine glands, giving one example of each. [4 marks]
(b) Copy and complete a table showing, for each of the following hormones, the gland that secretes it and one function: insulin, thyroxine, adrenaline, testosterone. [8 marks]
(c) State four differences between hormonal and nervous coordination. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Endocrine (ductless) glands release hormones directly into the blood, e.g. thyroid / pituitary / adrenal
2 marks: (a) Exocrine glands release secretions through ducts, e.g. salivary gland / sweat gland / pancreas (exocrine part)
2 marks: (b) Insulin - islets of Langerhans (pancreas) - lowers blood glucose / glucose to glycogen
2 marks: (b) Thyroxine - thyroid gland - controls metabolic rate / growth and development
2 marks: (b) Adrenaline - adrenal medulla - prepares body for emergency: increases heart rate, raises blood sugar
2 marks: (b) Testosterone - testes - development of male secondary sexual characteristics / sperm production
8 marks: (c) Any four, 2 marks each: hormonal uses chemical messengers, nervous uses electrical impulses; hormones transported in blood, impulses along neurones; hormonal response slow, nervous rapid; hormonal effects long-lasting, nervous short-lived; hormonal effects widespread, nervous localised
questions.explanation: (a) Endocrine glands are ductless and release hormones into blood (e.g. thyroid); exocrine glands pour secretions through ducts (e.g. salivary glands). (b) Insulin: pancreas, lowers blood sugar; thyroxine: thyroid, regulates metabolic rate; adrenaline: adrenal gland, fight-or-flight responses; testosterone: testes, male secondary sexual characteristics. (c) Hormonal coordination uses chemicals carried in blood, is slow, long-lasting and widespread; nervous coordination uses electrical impulses along nerves, is rapid, brief and localised.

questions.stem:
(a) Name six parts of the human eye and state one function of each. [12 marks]
(b) Explain how the eye adjusts to see a near object clearly. [4 marks]
(c) Name two defects of vision and state how each is corrected. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
12 marks: (a) Any six, 2 marks each: cornea - refracts light into the eye; iris - controls size of pupil / amount of light; pupil - admits light; lens - focuses light on the retina; retina - contains light-sensitive rods and cones; optic nerve - carries impulses to the brain; ciliary body - changes lens shape (accommodation); choroid - supplies blood / prevents internal reflection; sclera - protects and maintains shape; aqueous/vitreous humour - maintains shape and refracts light; yellow spot (fovea) - region of sharpest vision
2 marks: (b) Ciliary muscles contract and suspensory ligaments slacken
2 marks: (b) The elastic lens becomes thicker/more convex, increasing its refractive power, so the image is focused on the retina
4 marks: (c) Any two, 2 marks each: short sight (myopia) - concave/diverging lens; long sight (hypermetropia) - convex/converging lens; astigmatism - cylindrical lens; presbyopia - convex/bifocal lens; cataract - surgical removal of lens and replacement
questions.explanation: (a) The cornea refracts light; the iris regulates pupil size; the lens focuses light; the retina contains rods and cones; the optic nerve carries impulses to the brain; the ciliary body alters lens shape; the sclera protects the eye. (b) For near vision the ciliary muscles contract, the suspensory ligaments slacken and the lens becomes more convex, bending light more so the image falls on the retina. (c) Short sight is corrected with concave lenses and long sight with convex lenses.

questions.stem:
(a) Describe the events of the menstrual cycle in a woman, naming the hormones involved. [10 marks]
(b) State four functions of the placenta. [4 marks]
(c) Name three methods of birth control and explain how one of them works. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Menstruation (about days 1-5): breakdown and shedding of the uterine lining when progesterone falls
2 marks: (a) FSH from the pituitary stimulates development of a Graafian follicle, which secretes oestrogen
2 marks: (a) Oestrogen causes repair and thickening of the uterine lining
2 marks: (a) A surge of LH causes ovulation (about day 14 of a 28-day cycle); the follicle becomes the corpus luteum
2 marks: (a) Corpus luteum secretes progesterone, which maintains the lining; if no fertilisation, it degenerates and the cycle restarts
4 marks: (b) Any four, 1 mark each: exchange of oxygen and CO2; supplies nutrients to foetus; removes excretory wastes; secretes hormones (progesterone, oestrogen); passes antibodies to the foetus; acts as a barrier to some pathogens and keeps maternal and foetal blood separate
3 marks: (c) Any three methods, 1 mark each: condom; diaphragm; contraceptive pills; IUD; injectable contraceptive; vasectomy; tubal ligation; rhythm (safe period); abstinence
3 marks: (c) Correct explanation of one, e.g. condom is a rubber sheath that prevents sperms from entering the vagina and also reduces spread of STIs
questions.explanation: (a) Menstruation sheds the uterine lining. FSH stimulates a follicle, which secretes oestrogen to rebuild the lining. An LH surge triggers ovulation around day 14; the empty follicle becomes the corpus luteum, secreting progesterone to maintain the lining. Without fertilisation, the corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone falls and menstruation begins. (b) The placenta exchanges gases, supplies food, removes wastes, secretes hormones and passes antibodies. (c) Condom, pill, IUD; a condom traps semen so sperms cannot reach the ovum.

questions.stem:
(a) Define pollination and distinguish between self-pollination and cross-pollination. [4 marks]
(b) State four differences between insect-pollinated and wind-pollinated flowers. [8 marks]
(c) State four ways by which flowers are adapted to prevent self-pollination. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma
2 marks: (a) Self-pollination: to the stigma of the same flower or another flower on the same plant; cross-pollination: to the stigma of a flower on a different plant of the same species
8 marks: (b) Any four, 2 marks each: insect - large brightly coloured petals, wind - small dull or absent; insect - scent and nectar, wind - none; insect - sticky/rough heavy pollen, wind - light smooth abundant pollen; insect - stigma inside the flower, wind - feathery stigma hanging out; insect - anthers inside, wind - versatile anthers on long filaments
8 marks: (c) Any four, 2 marks each: protandry (stamens mature first); protogyny (stigma matures first); self-sterility/incompatibility; unisexual flowers (dioecious plants such as pawpaw); heterostyly / position of stigma above anthers (herkogamy)
questions.explanation: (a) Pollination is transfer of pollen from anther to stigma; self-pollination occurs within one flower or plant while cross-pollination is between different plants of the same species. (b) Insect-pollinated flowers are large, colourful, scented, with nectar, sticky pollen and enclosed stigmas; wind-pollinated flowers are small and dull with no scent or nectar, produce much light pollen and have feathery, exposed stigmas and dangling anthers. (c) Protandry, protogyny, self-incompatibility, separate male and female plants and structural separation of anthers and stigma.

questions.stem:
(a) Write a balanced chemical equation for photosynthesis. [2 marks]
(b) Describe the light and dark stages of photosynthesis. [8 marks]
(c) Describe an experiment to show that light is necessary for photosynthesis. [8 marks]
(d) State two ways in which the products of photosynthesis are used by the plant. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2 (in the presence of light and chlorophyll)
2 marks: (b) Light stage occurs in the grana; chlorophyll absorbs light energy
2 marks: (b) Water is split (photolysis) into hydrogen and oxygen; oxygen is released; ATP and reduced NADP are formed
2 marks: (b) Dark stage occurs in the stroma; does not need light directly
2 marks: (b) Carbon dioxide is reduced/fixed by hydrogen (from NADPH) using ATP to form carbohydrate (glucose)
2 marks: (c) Destarch a potted plant by keeping it in darkness for 48 hours; test one leaf to confirm no starch
2 marks: (c) Cover part of a leaf on both sides with black paper/aluminium foil; expose the plant to sunlight for some hours
2 marks: (c) Test the leaf for starch: boil in water, then in alcohol (over water bath), rinse and add iodine
2 marks: (c) Uncovered part turns blue-black, covered part brown (no starch): light is necessary for photosynthesis
2 marks: (d) Any two, 1 mark each: glucose used in respiration; stored as starch; converted to cellulose for cell walls; converted to proteins and fats; oxygen used in respiration / released
questions.explanation: (a) 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2. (b) In the light stage in the grana, chlorophyll absorbs light, water is split releasing oxygen, and ATP and NADPH are produced. In the dark stage in the stroma, ATP and NADPH are used to reduce CO2 to glucose. (c) A destarched plant with part of one leaf covered by foil is exposed to light; on testing with iodine only the uncovered part turns blue-black.
