(d) Glucose is respired for energy or converted to starch, cellulose, proteins and fats.

questions.stem:
(a) Describe the digestion of a meal of rice and beans from the mouth to the ileum in humans, naming the enzymes involved and their end products. [12 marks]
(b) State four properties of enzymes. [4 marks]
(c) Explain two ways in which the ileum is adapted for absorption. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Mouth: chewing breaks food into small pieces; salivary amylase converts starch (rice) to maltose
2 marks: (a) Stomach: hydrochloric acid provides acid medium; pepsin converts proteins (beans) to peptides/polypeptides
2 marks: (a) Duodenum: bile emulsifies fats; pancreatic amylase converts remaining starch to maltose
2 marks: (a) Duodenum: trypsin converts proteins/polypeptides to peptides; lipase converts fats to fatty acids and glycerol
2 marks: (a) Ileum: maltase converts maltose to glucose; sucrase and lactase act on sucrose and lactose
2 marks: (a) Ileum: peptidases (erepsin) convert peptides to amino acids; end products glucose, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol
4 marks: (b) Any four, 1 mark each: proteins; specific in action; work best at optimum temperature/pH; denatured by high temperature; catalysts not used up; reversible action; work in small amounts
4 marks: (c) Any two, 2 marks each: long and coiled - large surface area and time; numerous villi and microvilli - large surface area; thin epithelium - short diffusion distance; rich blood capillaries and lacteals - carry away absorbed food
questions.explanation: (a) In the mouth salivary amylase turns starch into maltose. In the stomach pepsin, in acid conditions, breaks protein into peptides. In the duodenum bile emulsifies fats, pancreatic amylase digests starch, trypsin digests proteins and lipase digests fats into fatty acids and glycerol. In the ileum maltase gives glucose and peptidases give amino acids. (b) Enzymes are proteins, specific, sensitive to temperature and pH, and unchanged at the end of the reaction. (c) The ileum is long with villi and microvilli, has a thin lining and a rich supply of capillaries and lacteals.

questions.stem:
(a) What is an ecological factor? [2 marks]
(b) Name two climatic, two edaphic and two biotic factors that affect organisms in a habitat. [6 marks]
(c) Name the instrument used to measure each of the following and state how one of them is used: (i) rainfall; (ii) relative humidity; (iii) wind speed; (iv) light intensity. [8 marks]
(d) Explain how temperature affects the distribution of organisms. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Any environmental condition (living or non-living) that affects the life, distribution and abundance of organisms in a habitat
2 marks: (b) Climatic: temperature, rainfall, light, humidity, wind (any two)
2 marks: (b) Edaphic: soil texture, pH, soil water, humus, soil air, mineral salts (any two)
2 marks: (b) Biotic: predation, competition, parasitism, disease, human activities (any two)
1 mark: (c)(i) Rain gauge
1 mark: (c)(ii) Hygrometer / wet and dry bulb thermometer
1 mark: (c)(iii) Anemometer
1 mark: (c)(iv) Light meter / photometer
4 marks: (c) Correct description of use of one instrument, e.g. rain gauge placed in an open place away from trees, water collected in 24 hours poured into a measuring cylinder and read in mm
2 marks: (d) Organisms survive only within a tolerance range of temperature; enzymes work best at an optimum and are inactivated or denatured outside it
2 marks: (d) Hence organisms are restricted to suitable regions or altitudes, or avoid extremes by migration, hibernation/aestivation or burrowing
questions.explanation: (a) An ecological factor is any living or non-living condition that affects organisms in a habitat. (b) Climatic: temperature and rainfall; edaphic: soil pH and texture; biotic: predation and competition. (c) Rainfall: rain gauge; humidity: hygrometer; wind speed: anemometer; light: light meter. A rain gauge is set in the open, and the water collected each 24 hours is measured in a graduated cylinder. (d) Each organism tolerates only a range of temperature because its enzymes work within limits, so species are confined to suitable zones or avoid extremes by migrating, hibernating or burrowing.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain the following terms: (i) allele; (ii) dominant character; (iii) phenotype. [6 marks]
(b) In a certain plant, red flower colour (R) is dominant over white (r). A heterozygous red-flowered plant is crossed with a white-flowered plant. Using a genetic diagram, show the genotypes and phenotypes of the F1 generation and state the phenotypic ratio. [8 marks]
(c) Two parents with the genotype AS have a child. Using a Punnett square, determine the probability that the child has sickle-cell anaemia. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) Allele: one of two or more alternative forms of a gene occupying the same locus on homologous chromosomes
2 marks: (a)(ii) Dominant character: one that is expressed in the phenotype even when only one allele for it is present (heterozygous condition)
2 marks: (a)(iii) Phenotype: the observable characteristics of an organism resulting from its genotype and the environment
2 marks: (b) Parents: Rr (red) x rr (white)
2 marks: (b) Gametes: R and r from the red parent; r and r from the white parent
2 marks: (b) F1 genotypes: Rr, Rr, rr, rr
2 marks: (b) Phenotypes: red and white; ratio 1 red : 1 white
2 marks: (c) Parents AS x AS; gametes A, S and A, S
2 marks: (c) Punnett square gives AA, AS, AS, SS
2 marks: (c) Probability of SS (sickle-cell anaemia) = 1/4 (25%)
questions.explanation: (a) An allele is an alternative form of a gene; a dominant character shows even in the heterozygote; the phenotype is the observable trait. (b) Rr x rr: gametes R, r and r; offspring Rr (red) and rr (white) in a 1 : 1 ratio. (c) AS x AS gives AA : AS : SS in the ratio 1 : 2 : 1, so the probability of an SS child is 1/4.

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between a food chain and a food web. [4 marks]
(b) In a grassland, grass is eaten by grasshoppers and rabbits; grasshoppers are eaten by lizards and birds; lizards and rabbits are eaten by snakes; birds are eaten by hawks. (i) Construct a food web from this information. (ii) Name the producer and one secondary consumer. (iii) State what would happen to the grass if all the snakes and hawks died, giving a reason. [10 marks]
(c) Explain why the biomass at each trophic level is usually less than the one below it. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) A food chain is a single linear sequence of feeding relationships through which energy passes from producers to consumers
2 marks: (a) A food web is a network of interconnected food chains in a community
4 marks: (b)(i) Correct web with arrows pointing from food to feeder: grass->grasshopper, grass->rabbit, grasshopper->lizard, grasshopper->bird, lizard->snake, rabbit->snake, bird->hawk (deduct for wrong arrows)
1 mark: (b)(ii) Producer: grass
1 mark: (b)(ii) Secondary consumer: lizard or bird (or snake via lizard)
2 marks: (b)(iii) Grass would decrease
2 marks: (b)(iii) Because rabbits, no longer eaten by snakes, increase in number and overgraze the grass
2 marks: (c) Energy is lost at each level as heat in respiration
2 marks: (c) Some material is not eaten (bones, roots) or not digested and lost in faeces
2 marks: (c) Only about 10% of energy/biomass is transferred, so less biomass can be supported at higher levels
questions.explanation: (a) A food chain is one linear feeding pathway; a food web is many interlinked chains. (b) Grass feeds grasshoppers and rabbits; grasshoppers feed lizards and birds; lizards and rabbits feed snakes; birds feed hawks. Grass is the producer and lizards or birds are secondary consumers. If snakes and hawks die, rabbits are no longer eaten, increase and overgraze, so the grass decreases. (c) At each level energy is lost as heat in respiration and in uneaten or undigested material, so only about 10% passes on and less biomass can be supported.

questions.stem:
(a) Describe the life cycle of the mosquito. [8 marks]
(b) Name the organism that causes malaria and explain how it is transmitted to humans. [4 marks]
(c) State four symptoms of malaria. [4 marks]
(d) State four measures that can be taken by a community to reduce the incidence of malaria. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Female lays eggs on the surface of still water (Anopheles singly with floats; Culex in rafts)
2 marks: (a) Eggs hatch into larvae (wrigglers) which feed on organic particles and breathe through a siphon/spiracles at the surface; they moult several times
2 marks: (a) Larva becomes a comma-shaped pupa (tumbler) which does not feed but breathes through respiratory trumpets
2 marks: (a) Adult emerges from the pupal case at the water surface; complete metamorphosis takes about 10-14 days
2 marks: (b) Plasmodium (e.g. Plasmodium falciparum), a protozoan
2 marks: (b) Infected female Anopheles mosquito injects sporozoites with saliva while sucking blood
4 marks: (c) Any four, 1 mark each: fever (high temperature); shivering/chills; headache; sweating; vomiting/nausea; loss of appetite; joint pains; anaemia
4 marks: (d) Any four, 1 mark each: drain stagnant water / clear gutters; clear bushes around homes; spray insecticides; use insecticide-treated nets; spray oil/larvicide on water; window and door nets; prompt treatment of patients; stock ponds with larva-eating fish; remove containers that hold water
questions.explanation: (a) Eggs laid on still water hatch into larvae that feed and breathe at the surface, moult and become comma-shaped pupae that do not feed; adults emerge after about 10-14 days. (b) Malaria is caused by Plasmodium, injected into the blood by an infected female Anopheles mosquito during feeding. (c) Fever, chills, headache, vomiting, joint pains and anaemia. (d) Draining stagnant water, clearing bushes, using treated nets, spraying insecticides and larvicides, and treating patients promptly.

questions.stem:
(a) What is conservation? [2 marks]
(b) List four natural resources in Nigeria and state one way of conserving each. [8 marks]
(c) State four problems associated with conservation of wildlife in West Africa. [4 marks]
(d) Name two agencies or bodies concerned with conservation and state one function of each. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) The careful management and wise use of natural resources to prevent waste, depletion or extinction so they remain available for future generations
8 marks: (b) Any four resource + method, 2 marks each: forest - afforestation/regulated felling/forest reserves; wildlife - game reserves/national parks/hunting laws; soil - crop rotation/cover crops/terracing/manuring; water - preventing pollution/dams/treatment; minerals and fossil fuels - recycling/efficient use/reducing gas flaring; fish - closed seasons/regulated net mesh size
4 marks: (c) Any four, 1 mark each: poaching/illegal hunting; deforestation and habitat loss; bush burning; lack of funds and personnel; poor enforcement of laws; ignorance of the public; urbanisation and farming encroachment; insecurity in reserves
6 marks: (d) Any two, 3 marks each (1 name, 2 function): National Park Service - manages national parks; Forestry departments/Forestry Research Institute of Nigeria - forest reserves and research; Nigerian Conservation Foundation - education and conservation projects; WWF/IUCN - funding and listing endangered species; NESREA - enforcement of environmental standards
questions.explanation: (a) Conservation is the wise management of natural resources to prevent their depletion. (b) Forests are conserved by afforestation and controlled felling, wildlife by parks and hunting laws, soil by cover crops and terracing, water by preventing pollution, and fish by closed seasons and net mesh regulation. (c) Problems include poaching, habitat destruction, bush burning, poor funding and weak enforcement. (d) The National Park Service manages national parks; the Nigerian Conservation Foundation runs conservation education and projects.

questions.stem:
(a) Outline the theory of evolution proposed by (i) Lamarck; (ii) Darwin. [10 marks]
(b) State three objections to Lamarck's theory. [3 marks]
(c) Explain how each of the following provides evidence of evolution: (i) fossils; (ii) homologous structures; (iii) comparative embryology. [6 marks]
(d) Give one modern example of natural selection. [1 mark]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) Lamarck: organs that are used regularly develop and become larger (use)
2 marks: (a)(i) Organs that are not used degenerate (disuse); these acquired characteristics are passed to offspring, e.g. long neck of giraffe
2 marks: (a)(ii) Darwin: organisms produce more offspring than can survive; populations remain fairly constant; there is a struggle for existence
2 marks: (a)(ii) Individuals vary, and those with favourable variations survive (survival of the fittest / natural selection)
2 marks: (a)(ii) Survivors reproduce and pass on favourable variations; over many generations new species arise
3 marks: (b) Any three, 1 mark each: acquired characteristics are not inherited (e.g. body-builder's muscles); Weismann cut tails of mice for many generations yet tails persisted; changes in body cells do not affect genes in gametes; no mechanism of inheritance shown
2 marks: (c)(i) Fossils in successive rock layers show gradual changes in organisms from simple to complex over time
2 marks: (c)(ii) Homologous structures (e.g. pentadactyl limb) have the same basic plan but different functions, indicating a common ancestor
2 marks: (c)(iii) Embryos of different vertebrates look alike at early stages (gill slits, tail), suggesting common ancestry
1 mark: (d) Any one: resistance of bacteria to antibiotics; resistance of mosquitoes to insecticides; resistance of Plasmodium to chloroquine; industrial melanism in peppered moth
questions.explanation: (a) Lamarck proposed that use enlarges organs and disuse weakens them, and these acquired changes are inherited. Darwin proposed overproduction, struggle for existence, variation, survival of the fittest and inheritance of favourable variations, producing new species over time. (b) Acquired traits are not inherited; cutting mouse tails for generations did not shorten tails; body cell changes do not alter gametes. (c) Fossils show gradual change; homologous structures indicate common ancestry; similar early embryos suggest descent from a common ancestor. (d) Antibiotic resistance in bacteria.

questions.stem:
(a) Describe the nitrogen cycle in nature, naming the organisms involved at each stage. [12 marks]
(b) Explain why leguminous crops such as cowpea and groundnut are used to improve soil fertility. [4 marks]
(c) State two human activities that add nitrogen compounds to the soil and two that remove them. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Atmospheric nitrogen is fixed into nitrates by lightning (nitrogen + oxygen form oxides that dissolve in rain)
2 marks: (a) Nitrogen-fixing bacteria: free-living (Azotobacter, Clostridium) and symbiotic (Rhizobium in legume root nodules); also blue-green algae (Nostoc)
2 marks: (a) Plants absorb nitrates and make proteins; animals obtain proteins by eating plants
2 marks: (a) Death and excretion: putrefying bacteria and fungi convert proteins, urea into ammonia/ammonium compounds (ammonification)
2 marks: (a) Nitrification: Nitrosomonas converts ammonium to nitrites; Nitrobacter converts nitrites to nitrates
2 marks: (a) Denitrification: denitrifying bacteria (e.g. Pseudomonas) convert nitrates to nitrogen gas, especially in waterlogged soils
2 marks: (b) Their root nodules contain Rhizobium, which fixes atmospheric nitrogen into nitrogen compounds
2 marks: (b) When roots and residues decay or are ploughed in, nitrogen compounds are released into the soil for the next crop
2 marks: (c) Add: application of nitrogenous fertilisers / manure / growing legumes (any two)
2 marks: (c) Remove: crop harvesting; leaching through bush clearing; bush burning; erosion (any two)
questions.explanation: (a) Lightning and nitrogen-fixing bacteria (Azotobacter, Rhizobium) convert atmospheric nitrogen to nitrogen compounds. Plants absorb nitrates and build proteins, which pass to animals. Decomposers convert proteins and wastes into ammonia; Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter oxidise this to nitrite then nitrate; denitrifying bacteria return nitrogen gas to the air. (b) Legume nodules hold Rhizobium, which fixes nitrogen; decay of residues enriches the soil. (c) Fertilisers and manure add nitrogen; harvesting, leaching, burning and erosion remove it.
